en: The Buddha’s teaching, the Buddha’s teaching, is the dance.

The triad consisting of dance (*nṛtta*), song (*gīta*), and instrumental music (*vādya*) is called *nāṭya*, and also *tauryatrika*. The most ancient Āryas were connoisseurs of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) not only in the science of literature (*sāhityavidyā*) but also in the science of drama (*nāṭyavidyā*). Its source text is known as the *Nāṭyaveda*. It was composed by the sage Bharata approximately two thousand years ago. The teacher Abhinavagupta, who lived around the year 4100 [of the Kali era], composed an extensive commentary on it titled the *Abhinavabhāratī*.

When the Buddha’s teaching was proclaimed and caste restrictions were disregarded, as thousands of years passed, Kṣatriyas devoted to the profession of heroes and Vaiśyas devoted to the profession of trade began to employ Brāhmaṇas as proxies for Vedic sacrificial rites. As the practice of employing proxies increased, their excessive respect for Brāhmaṇas grew; however, due to a lack of the sense of necessity regarding the study of the Vedas, there was a decline in such engagement.

Knowledge of the Vedas and Shastras became dependent solely upon the Brahmins; and many Brahmins, satisfied by easily obtained honor, no longer maintained their former faith in the diligent cultivation of learning.

Thus, as the practice of knowledge declined, the virtuous qualities rooted in that knowledge became rare among all the social orders (*varṇas*). Gradually, their mutual affection, their impartiality, and the realization that "the four orders constitute a single family" came to an end. On the contrary, contempt for the lower orders by the higher orders arose, and envy toward the higher orders sprouted among them. Furthermore, the conduct of the social orders became increasingly burdened with a multitude of vices.

At this juncture, the doctrine of the Buddha appeared in India. Because of its absence of caste restrictions, this doctrine became a source of great consolation for those suffering under the affliction of caste rules, as if providing release from imprisonment. Even some Brahmins at that time accepted this doctrine upon seeing its merits, let alone others.

Renunciation of worldly pleasures, non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, tranquility, equanimity, compassion for living beings, altruism, and the protection of those seeking refuge—these qualities and practices were its very essence.

In this system, the doctrines are taught according to the view of the Brāhmaṇas; likewise, heaven and hell, the gods, rebirth, and liberation—also known by the name *nirvāṇa*—are accepted in this system. However, the sacrifice to the Lord through the slaughter of living beings, which is admitted in the Brāhmaṇa doctrine, is utterly condemned in this system. The essential principles of the Buddha’s teaching are taught in the *Śṛgālavāda-sūtra* and the *Mahārāhula-sūtra*.

This doctrine, which sprouted in the latter half of the twenty-sixth century of the Kali age, spread across the whole of India through the efforts of great monks and kings, and subsequently gained a foothold in China, Japan, and Lanka; today, however, it survives only in a very rare form within India.

Long ago, in the city of Kapilavastu in Nepal, there was a king named Śuddhodana in the lineage of the Śākya kṣatriyas. Desiring progeny for a long time, he begot a son named Siddhārtha upon Queen Māyā in the year 2544 of the Kali age. This lineage—

He was known by the name "Gautama," by his clan name as "Śākyamuni," and was renowned as "Buddha" due to his realization of the Truth. On the seventh day after he was separated from his mother, his maternal aunt Gautamī raised him. Having completed his studies and reached youth, he married a Śākya maiden named Gopā and begot a son named Rāhula through her.

Becoming disenchanted with the pleasures of kingship due to an extremely firm contemplation on the transience of human enjoyments, he went forth into homelessness one night while the women of the inner apartments were fast asleep.

First, having reached Girivraja, he properly acquired the principles of the noble teachings from wandering mendicants dwelling in the caves there. Seeing that his desired happiness had not been attained by that much alone, he began to practice severe austerities at Buddhagayā.

While practicing such austerities, after six years had passed, on a certain day he fell into a swoon due to excessive exhaustion; and when consciousness was regained in an instant, he brought his asceticism to an end.

Then, having reached the bank of the Phalgu river, when he sat down at the foot of a certain Bodhi tree, all the events of his previous births appeared to him, and the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) was awakened within him.

Subsequently, the Buddha gained many disciples in Kāśī and Uruvilvā. Accompanied by his disciples, this passionless sage, performing pure deeds for the sake of others, led people here and there into his own doctrine, disregarding distinctions of caste through his teachings whose sole essence was virtue.

Being honored exceedingly by King Bimbisāra in Magadha, he dwelt there for a long time. Then, desiring once more to see his father, he went to the city of Kapilavastu and initiated his own son, Rāhula, into his doctrine. After his father’s passing, he caused his maternal aunt and his wife to don the saffron robes. Thus, having established imperishable fame throughout the world, the Sage attained *nirvāṇa* in the year 2624 of the Kali era. The Purāṇas proclaim this Sage to be an incarnation of Viṣṇu.
